Q194. What is a tool sandbox and why is it essential for code-executing agents?

Any agent that executes code must run in an isolated environment:

# Dangerous
subprocess.run(code_from_llm, shell=True)

# Safer
docker_result = docker_client.containers.run(
    "python:3.11-slim",
    command=["python", "-c", code_from_llm],
    network_mode="none",          # No internet
    mem_limit="256m",             # Memory capped
    cpu_period=100000,
    cpu_quota=50000,              # 50% CPU
    remove=True,
    timeout=10
)

Always: no network access, memory/CPU limits, ephemeral filesystem, execution timeout.

•

Q195. What is the chain-of-verification (CoVe) technique?

After generating an initial response, the agent generates verification questions and answers them to check for errors:

Initial answer → "The Eiffel Tower was built in 1887"
Verification questions:
  Q: When was the Eiffel Tower construction started?
  A: Search → 1887 (construction) ✓
  Q: When was it completed/opened?
  A: Search → 1889 ✗ (original said 1887 was completion)
Final corrected answer → "Built 1887-1889, opened 1889"

Reduces hallucination by forcing the agent to cross-check its claims.

•

Q196. What is tool chaining vs tool composition?

Tool chainingTool composition

Tool chaining: Output of one tool becomes input to the next.

search→results"Python tutorials"
summarize→summaryresults

Tool composition: Combine multiple primitive tools into a higher-level tool.

@tool
def research_and_summarize(topic: str) -> str:
    results = search(topic)
    return summarize(results)

Tool composition reduces planning complexity and improves reliability for common workflows.

•

Q197. What are the key considerations for agent system design review?

Checklist for reviewing an agent system before production: - [ ] Defined scope and exit conditions - [ ] All tool inputs/outputs are validated - [ ] Cost limits and step limits are enforced - [ ] HITL required for irreversible actions - [ ] Full observability (traces, metrics, logs) - [ ] Error handling for every failure mode - [ ] Security review: prompt injection, tool sandboxing - [ ] Data privacy: PII handling in memory and logs - [ ] Load testing: concurrent agent runs - [ ] Rollback plan for agent regressions

•

Q198. What is progressive disclosure in agent UX design?

Default viewSummary viewDetail viewDebug view

Show users progressively more detail as needed: 1. Default view: Just the final answer 2. Summary view: Key steps taken 3. Detail view: Full reasoning trace 4. Debug view: Raw tool calls and LLM inputs/outputs

Aligns with user needs — most users want the answer; power users and engineers want the trace.

•

Q199. What is the future of agentic AI? Key research directions.

ReliabilityLong horizonsWorld modelsAgent learningMulti-agent coordinationTrust and safety
  1. Reliability: Getting success rate from 30% to 80%+ on hard benchmarks (SWE-bench)
  2. Long horizons: Maintaining coherent goals over days/weeks of operation
  3. World models: Better internal simulation for planning before acting
  4. Agent learning: Online reinforcement from task outcomes
  5. Multi-agent coordination: Scalable, robust multi-agent protocols
  6. Trust and safety: Alignment at the agent level, not just the LLM level
•

Q200. How do you design a cost-effective, production-grade agentic system from scratch?

  1. Define task types and complexity distribution → Classify tasks by cost/complexity
  2. Start with the minimal architecture → Single agent, minimal tools
  3. Evaluate on held-out task set → Benchmark: success rate, cost, latency
  4. Identify failure modes from traces → Add tools/complexity only where needed
  5. Add observability before scaling → LangSmith / Phoenix tracing
  6. Implement guardrails → Step limits, cost limits, HITL for risky actions
  7. Gradual rollout → Canary: 5% traffic → 20% → 50% → 100%
  8. Monitor continuously → Cost/task, success rate, latency P99
Operations at Scale, Budgets & Guardrails (Q201–Q204)
•

Q201. Your agent is getting heavy traffic (high QPS). How do you handle it?

Admission control & backpressureProtect the LLM providersemantically cachePerceived latencyObserve & shed

First, the key intuition: an agent request is not one LLM call. It is a multi-step loop — N LLM calls + M tool calls + retries — so each "request" is 5–50× heavier, slower, and more stateful than a chat completion. Scaling agents = scaling a long-running, stateful, expensive workflow, not a stateless endpoint. The strategy is: decouple, make stateless, queue, autoscale, and protect downstream.

Layers, in order of impact:

  1. Decouple from the request thread (queue). Never run the agent loop synchronously inside the HTTP handler — one slow task blocks a worker for 30s+. Accept → enqueue → return a job_id → process asynchronously (Celery/SQS/Temporal). Clients poll or get a webhook/SSE on completion.
  2. Stateless workers + externalized state. Keep agent state (plan, history, tool results) in a checkpointer (Postgres/Redis), not in process memory. Then any worker can resume any task, and you can scale workers freely. See [[checkpointing]].
  3. Horizontal autoscaling on queue depth (KEDA/HPA scaling on backlog, not CPU — the bottleneck is I/O waiting on the LLM, not CPU).
  4. Admission control & backpressure. Per-tenant token-bucket rate limit + a cap on max concurrent agents. When saturated, return 429 / queue-position rather than melting down. Degrading cleanly beats falling over.
  5. Protect the LLM provider. Respect provider RPM/TPM limits, exponential backoff + jitter on 429s, batch where possible, and semantically cache LLM/tool results so repeated sub-steps don't re-call. Route cheap steps (routing, classification) to a smaller model.
  6. Perceived latency. Stream partial output, show progress ("searching… analyzing…"), and parallelize independent tool calls.
  7. Observe & shed. Track queue depth, P99 latency, tokens/task, success rate; alert and load-shed before the provider rate-limits you.
import time

class TokenBucket:
    """Per-tenant admission control. Refills at `rate` tokens/sec, capacity `burst`."""
    def __init__(self, rate: float, burst: int):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, burst
        self.tokens = burst
        self.ts = time.monotonic()

    def allow(self, cost: int = 1) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.ts) * self.rate)
        self.ts = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False   # caller returns 429 / enqueues with backpressure

# API boundary:
#   if not bucket.allow(): return 429
#   job_id = queue.enqueue(run_agent, task)   # async worker picks it up
#   return {"job_id": job_id}

Relates to [[scaling-concurrent-agents]] (Q88) and [[rate-limiting]] (Scenario Q2).

•

Q202. What happens when the budget is over (cost/token/step budget exceeded mid-task)?

circuit breakerdegrade gracefully, not crashPre-check, don't post-mortemUse the escape hatchCheckpoint so it's resumableTiered thresholds

Intuition: an agent loops autonomously, so without a hard budget it can run away — an infinite tool loop or a goal-drift spiral generates unbounded cost. A budget is the circuit breaker that bounds a single task. You define a budget per task across several axes — max $, max tokens, max steps, and max wall-clock — and check it before each step.

Crucially, exceeding the budget should degrade gracefully, not crash:

  • Pre-check, don't post-mortem. Before each LLM/tool call, ask "will the next step exceed the remaining budget?" If yes, stop the loop before spending.
  • Return best partial result + a flag. Hand back the best answer reached so far with status: "budget_exhausted", complete: false — never a silent failure or a raw exception to the user.
  • Use the escape hatch. Escalate to a human / flag_for_review rather than guessing (see [[agentic-escape-hatch]], Q130).
  • Checkpoint so it's resumable. Save state; if the budget is topped up (or a human approves more), resume from where it stopped instead of restarting.
  • Tiered thresholds. Warn at 80%, downgrade to a cheaper model, then hard-stop at 100% — soft degradation before the cliff.
  • Two scopes: per-task budget (this run) and per-tenant quota (monthly spend). The tenant quota is enforced at the API boundary (429 / quota exceeded), separate from the per-task circuit breaker.
class BudgetExceeded(Exception): ...

class BudgetTracker:
    def __init__(self, max_usd: float, max_steps: int, max_seconds: float):
        self.max_usd, self.max_steps, self.max_seconds = max_usd, max_steps, max_seconds
        self.spent_usd = 0.0
        self.steps = 0
        self.start = time.monotonic()

    def check(self) -> None:
        """Call BEFORE each agent step; raises so the loop stops cleanly."""
        if self.spent_usd >= self.max_usd:        raise BudgetExceeded("cost")
        if self.steps >= self.max_steps:          raise BudgetExceeded("steps")
        if time.monotonic() - self.start >= self.max_seconds: raise BudgetExceeded("time")

    def charge(self, usd: float) -> None:
        self.spent_usd += usd
        self.steps += 1

# Agent loop:
#   try:
#       while not done:
#           budget.check()                 # stop before overspending
#           obs, cost = run_step(state)
#           budget.charge(cost)
#   except BudgetExceeded as e:
#       return {"status": "budget_exhausted", "reason": str(e),
#               "partial_answer": best_so_far, "resumable_state": checkpoint}

Relates to [[cost-optimization]] (Scenario Q15) and the cost-limit guardrail in Q200.

•

Q203. What are the challenges between two agents (multi-agent coordination)?

Inconsistent / stale world viewsWrite conflicts / race conditionsDeadlock & communication stormsGoal misalignment & redundant workTrust boundary & error propagationcompound

When two (or more) agents collaborate, the failure modes are fundamentally coordination problems — the same class of bugs you see in distributed systems, now with non-deterministic actors:

  • Inconsistent / stale world views. Each agent acts on its own snapshot of state; agent B proceeds on data agent A has already invalidated → incoherent results.
  • Write conflicts / race conditions on shared state when agents run in parallel and both mutate the same field.
  • Deadlock & communication storms. Two agents wait on each other, or ping-pong clarifying questions forever, burning tokens with no progress.
  • Goal misalignment & redundant work. Without clear ownership, two agents do the same subtask (wasted cost) or each assumes the other owns a step (gap).
  • Trust boundary & error propagation. Should agent B blindly trust agent A's output? One agent's hallucination becomes another's input, and errors compound across the chain.
  • Handoff/context loss. Information drops between agents when the handoff isn't structured.
  • Cost & latency blowup. More agents = more LLM calls; an N-agent debate can be N× the cost.
  • Debuggability. Non-determinism × multiple actors makes failures hard to reproduce.

Mitigations: a single source of truth (shared typed state / blackboard with explicit field ownership + optimistic locking), a structured handoff protocol (Q50), a supervisor/orchestrator with clear routing (Q151) instead of free-for-all peer chatter, hard round/message limits + timeouts (Q53), independent verification of high-stakes cross-agent outputs (Q48), and distributed tracing with shared trace IDs (Scenario Q43).

from typing import TypedDict

class SharedState(TypedDict):
    plan: str         # OWNED by planner   — only planner writes
    findings: str     # OWNED by researcher
    draft: str        # OWNED by writer
    turn_count: int   # guard against communication storms

def step(state: SharedState, max_turns: int = 12) -> SharedState:
    if state["turn_count"] >= max_turns:
        raise RuntimeError("round limit hit — likely a coordination loop")
    state["turn_count"] += 1
    return state

Builds on [[multi-agent-coordination]] (Q46) and [[trust-boundary]] (Q48).

•

Q204. What are guardrails, and how did you use them?

defense in depthInputTool / actionLoop / resourcebudget/cost capOutput

Guardrails are the deterministic safety/validation layer wrapped around a probabilistic agent. The LLM decides; guardrails enforce hard boundaries on what it may see, what it may do, and what it may say. You can't trust the model to police itself, so you put independent, testable checks at every boundary — defense in depth.

The four boundaries (where guardrails sit):

BoundaryGuardrailCatches
InputPII/secret detection, prompt-injection classifier, jailbreak/off-topic filter, max input sizeMalicious or malformed user input
Tool / actionTool allowlist, argument schema validation, least-privilege creds, sandboxing, HITL approval for irreversible actions, blast-radius limitsDangerous or out-of-scope actions
Loop / resourceMax steps, budget/cost cap (Q202), timeout, loop detectionRunaway cost / infinite loops
OutputSchema/format validation, PII redaction, toxicity/policy classifier, groundedness check, competitor/legal-claim filterUnsafe or non-compliant responses

How I used them (customer-support agent): I layered all four. (1) Input — an injection/PII filter scrubbed the user message before it hit the model. (2) Tool — the agent had an allowlist of tools with a read-only DB connection, and refunds/outbound emails required HITL approval. (3) Resource — a per-task step + cost budget circuit breaker. (4) Output — a policy classifier + PII redaction ran on every response, and the answer had to be grounded in retrieved policy docs or it was blocked. Every violation was logged and routed to human review (the log is the dataset that improves the guardrails), and policies lived in a database so they could change without a redeploy. Tooling: NeMo Guardrails / Guardrails AI for structure, Llama Guard for content classification, plus regex + schema validation for the deterministic checks.

def guarded_agent(user_input: str):
    # 1. INPUT guardrail
    if injection_detector(user_input) or contains_pii(user_input):
        return block("input rejected")

    # 2 & 3. TOOL + RESOURCE guardrails live inside the loop
    result = run_agent_loop(
        user_input,
        allowed_tools=TOOL_ALLOWLIST,          # tool guardrail
        validate_args=schema_validate,         # arg guardrail
        require_approval={"send_email", "issue_refund"},  # HITL
        budget=BudgetTracker(max_usd=0.50, max_steps=10, max_seconds=30),
    )

    # 4. OUTPUT guardrail
    if policy_violation(result.text) or not is_grounded(result.text, result.context):
        log_for_review(result); return escalate_to_human(result)
    return redact_pii(result.text)

Builds on [[prompt-injection-defense]] (Q60/Q108), [[hitl]] (Q56–Q58), and the cost-limit guardrail in Q200. The RAG-specific guardrail (faithfulness / "I don't know" gate) is covered in 05_RAG_and_Vector_Stores.md §20.

Real-World Production Incidents (Q205–Q211)

Incident-style questions. Answer each in the same shape an on-call engineer thinks: symptom → likely root causes → immediate mitigation → permanent fix/prevention.

•

Q205. Incident: P99 latency spiked and agents are timing out, though P50 looks fine.

Symptom shapeLikely causesImmediatePermanentalert on P99 + queue depth
  • Symptom shape: median is healthy, tail is on fire → a subset of tasks are pathological, not the whole system.
  • Likely causes: a few tasks hit the max-step ceiling (long loops); one downstream tool got slow and the agent retries it serially; LLM provider latency variance on long-context calls; queue backlog so tasks wait before they even start (queue time counted as latency).
  • Immediate: shed load (backpressure/429), cap per-task steps and per-tool timeouts so a slow tool can't stall the whole loop, fail fast on the slow tool with a fallback.
  • Permanent: parallelize independent tool calls, add per-tool circuit breakers, separate fast and slow task classes onto different queues/worker pools, and alert on P99 + queue depth, not just averages — averages hide tail pain.
•

Q206. Incident: cost spiked 5× overnight with no traffic increase.

Likely causesImmediatebudget circuit breakerPermanentcost-per-tasksteps-per-task
  • Likely causes: runaway loops (agents not converging, hitting max steps every time); a prompt/model change that ballooned token usage; a poisoned/looping input class; retry storms against a failing tool (each retry = full LLM call); caching silently broke (cache miss rate → 100%).
  • Immediate: check tokens-per-task and steps-per-task dashboards for the spike window; enforce/clamp the per-task budget circuit breaker (Q202); kill the offending task class; verify the cache is actually hitting.
  • Permanent: alert on cost-per-task and steps-per-task (not just total spend — total spend alerts fire too late), loop detection, and a canary that catches token regressions before deploy.
•

Q207. Incident: a downstream tool/API the agent depends on is failing (errors or timeouts) in production.

The trapImmediatecircuit breakerPermanent
  • The trap: the agent treats the failure as a normal observation, "reasons" about it, and either loops retrying or hallucinates a result to keep going.
  • Immediate: circuit breakerafter K failures, stop calling the tool and route to a fallback ("this data source is unavailable") instead of letting every agent retry it. Return a degraded but honest answer.
  • Permanent: wrap tools with retry + backoff + jitter and a breaker; feed structured errors back to the LLM ("tool X is down — do not retry; proceed without it"); add a health check that disables the tool fleet-wide; cache last-good results to serve during outages.
class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, fail_max=5, reset_after=60):
        self.fail_max, self.reset_after = fail_max, reset_after
        self.fails, self.opened_at = 0, None
    def allow(self) -> bool:
        if self.opened_at and time.monotonic() - self.opened_at < self.reset_after:
            return False                       # circuit OPEN → skip the tool, use fallback
        return True
    def record(self, ok: bool):
        if ok: self.fails, self.opened_at = 0, None
        else:
            self.fails += 1
            if self.fails >= self.fail_max: self.opened_at = time.monotonic()
•

Q208. Incident: the LLM provider is rate-limiting you (429s) or having an outage (5xx) during peak.

Immediatefail overPermanent
  • Immediate: exponential backoff + jitter on 429/5xx; shed non-critical traffic; serve from semantic cache where possible; if you have a secondary provider, fail over to it.
  • Permanent: provision a TPM/RPM headroom budget and rate-limit yourself below the provider ceiling so you never hit it; multi-provider abstraction with automatic failover; degrade gracefully (smaller model, cached answer, or "try again shortly") rather than erroring; queue + retry async tasks so transient outages are invisible to users.
•

Q209. Incident: a harmful / non-compliant agent output reached a user despite guardrails. How do you respond?

ContainAssess blast radiusRoot-causePatchPrevent regression

Treat it like a security incident, not a bug:

  1. Contain: kill-switch the affected agent/flow or force it into HITL/draft-only mode immediately.
  2. Assess blast radius: query logs for how many users hit it and how (the audit log from Q204 is what makes this possible).
  3. Root-cause: which guardrail layer should have caught it and why didn't it (gap in the classifier? a new attack phrasing? a prompt change disabled a check?).
  4. Patch: add the failing case to the guardrail test set, tighten the specific layer (input filter / output classifier), redeploy.
  5. Prevent regression: the incident case becomes a permanent test; review whether this class of action should require HITL going forward.

Key point: guardrails are layered precisely because any single one will eventually be bypassed — the response is to strengthen the layer and add the case to the eval set, not to claim it "can't happen again."

•

Q210. Incident: a prompt-injection attack is discovered in production (e.g., a retrieved doc or tool output hijacked the agent).

ImmediatePermanentuntrusted data, never instructions
  • Immediate: disable the compromised data source/tool; revoke any credentials the agent could have leaked; scan logs for what actions the hijacked agent took (and roll them back if reversible).
  • Permanent: treat all external content (retrieved docs, tool outputs, web pages) as untrusted data, never instructions — delimit it and instruct the model never to follow instructions found inside it; add an injection classifier on tool outputs (not just user input); enforce least-privilege so a hijacked agent can't perform high-impact actions without HITL; sandbox tools. See Q60/Q108.
•

Q211. Incident: a model/version upgrade silently degraded agent quality (a regression you didn't catch before rollout).

SymptomWhy it happensImmediatePermanentevaluation-driven development
  • Symptom: success rate or tool-selection accuracy drops after a model swap, even though "it's a better model."
  • Why it happens: agents are sensitive to prompt/format behavior; a new model parses tool schemas or follows the system prompt differently, so traces that used to pass now fail.
  • Immediate: roll back to the pinned previous model version (always pin model IDs in prod — never float).
  • Permanent: evaluation-driven development (Q110) — every model/prompt change runs against a held-out eval set with success rate, tool accuracy, cost, and latency, gated in CI; canary the new version on 5% of traffic and compare metrics (Q115) before full rollout. Non-determinism means you compare distributions over repeated runs, not single outputs (Q114).
